Reading from and writing to files — and handling the things that go wrong in the process — is what turns a script into a useful tool. This post covers Python's open() function, the with context manager, the modern pathlib API, exception handling, and how to define your own exceptions. It closes the base Python course; future posts extend into stdlib deep-dives, typing, async, and packaging.
Series map: 00 Setup → 01 Syntax → 02 Data Structures → 03 Functions & Modules → 04 OOP → 05 Files & Exceptions (this post) → (future: stdlib, typing, async, packaging, testing).

Open, read, and write text and binary files.
Use the with statement (context manager) — and understand why it matters.
Use pathlib.Path for cross-platform path manipulation.
Read structured formats: csv, json.
Handle exceptions with try/except/else/finally.
Raise built-in and custom exceptions.
Avoid the classic "catch everything" anti-pattern.

# Read entire file into a string
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
text = f.read()
# Read line by line (memory-efficient for big files)
with open("log.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
for line in f:
print(line.rstrip()) # rstrip removes trailing \n
# Read all lines into a list
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
lines = f.readlines()

with open("out.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
f.write("hello\n")
f.write("world\n")

Mode · Meaning
"r" · read (default) — file must exist
"w" · write — truncates existing, creates if missing
"a" · append — adds to end, creates if missing
"x" · exclusive create — fails if file exists
"b" · binary (combine: "rb", "wb")
"+" · read + write ("r+", "w+")

# WITHOUT with — must remember to close
f = open("x.txt")
data = f.read()
f.close() # easy to forget; missed on exceptions
# WITH — auto-closes even on exception
with open("x.txt") as f:
data = f.read()
# closed here, no matter what
The with block is a context manager: the file is guaranteed to be closed when the block exits. Always use it for files.
Where I got stuck: an early script of mine kept thousands of files open until the OS refused new ones. The fix was 5 characters: wrap the open(...) in a with. I never forgot again.

Always pass encoding="utf-8" when opening text files. Without it, Python uses the OS default (cp1252 on Windows, utf-8 on macOS/Linux) → cross-platform bugs.
with open("name.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
f.write("São Paulo\n")
For binary files (images, executables, etc.), use "rb" / "wb" — no encoding needed:
with open("image.png", "rb") as f:
data = f.read() # bytes

Avoid string concatenation for paths. Use pathlib.Path:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("data") / "users" / "ada.json"
# Path('data/users/ada.json') — works on every OS
p.exists() # bool
p.is_file() # bool
p.is_dir() # bool
p.name # 'ada.json'
p.stem # 'ada'
p.suffix # '.json'
p.parent # Path('data/users')
p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
p.write_text("hello", encoding="utf-8")
p.read_bytes()
p.write_bytes(b"\x00\xff")
# iterate directory
for child in Path(".").iterdir():
print(child)
# recursive glob
for f in Path(".").rglob("*.py"):
print(f)

p.absolute() # absolute path
p.resolve() # absolute + follow symlinks
p.relative_to("/home") # path relative to another
p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
p.unlink() # delete file
p.rename("new_name")
Trick: Path.read_text() and Path.write_text() are perfect for small files. No need for open() at all. data = Path("config.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8") is a one-liner.

import json
# write
data = {"name": "Ada", "tags": ["mathematician", "engineer"]}
with open("user.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
# read
with open("user.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
loaded = json.load(f)
# str <-> dict
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
parsed = json.loads(text)

import csv
# write
rows = [["name", "age"], ["Ada", 30], ["Bob", 25]]
with open("users.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
writer = csv.writer(f)
writer.writerows(rows)
# read with header → dict per row
with open("users.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
reader = csv.DictReader(f)
for row in reader:
print(row["name"], row["age"])
Trick: always pass newline="" to CSV open() calls. Without it, Windows can write extra blank lines. Trust me, that bug is a 30-minute mystery the first time.

An exception is an error event that interrupts normal flow. Python signals problems by raising exceptions.
1 / 0
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
int("abc")
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
open("missing.txt")
# FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'
d = {"a": 1}
d["b"]
# KeyError: 'b'
If unhandled, the exception propagates up the call stack and (eventually) crashes the program with a traceback.

try:
n = int(input("Number: "))
result = 100 / n
except ValueError:
print("Not a valid integer")
except ZeroDivisionError:
print("Can't divide by zero")
except (TypeError, OverflowError) as e:
print(f"Other error: {e}")
else:
print(f"Result: {result}") # runs only if no exception
finally:
print("done") # runs always
Parts:
try: — code that might fail.
except XError: — handle a specific exception.
except (A, B) as e: — multiple types + bind to name.
else: — runs if try completed without exception.
finally: — always runs (cleanup).

try:
do_stuff()
except: # NEVER do this
pass
try:
do_stuff()
except Exception: # better, but still wide
log_error()
A bare except: catches everything, including KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C) and SystemExit. You will eventually trap a signal you wanted to receive.
Rule of thumb: catch the narrowest exception type that addresses the failure. If you don't know the type, run the code, see the traceback, then catch that type.

def withdraw(account, amount):
if amount <= 0:
raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
if amount > account.balance:
raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
account.balance -= amount
Use built-in exceptions when they fit:
Exception · Use when
ValueError · A value is wrong type/range
TypeError · An argument has wrong type
KeyError / IndexError · Missing dict key / out-of-range index
FileNotFoundError · File not found
RuntimeError · Generic runtime issue
NotImplementedError · Method must be overridden

You've used with open(...). You can write your own context manager — useful for resource setup/teardown (DB connections, locks, temp directories).
from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def timer(label):
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
try:
yield # block body runs here
finally:
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"{label}: {elapsed:.3f}s")
with timer("load"):
data = Path("big.csv").read_text()
The block runs at the yield. Whatever's before/after runs as setup/teardown — even on exceptions thanks to the try/finally.
Given a directory, find all .txt files. For each line that appears in more than one file, print the line and the files it appears in.
Use @dataclass for Account, custom exceptions for InsufficientFunds and AccountNotFound, and a Bank class with transfer(from_id, to_id, amount). Persist accounts to a JSON file on each operation.

Write text · Path("f.txt").write_text("...", encoding="utf-8")

JSON write · json.dumps(o, indent=2) / json.dump(o, f)
